# Recommender Systems


A **recommender system** (also called a recommendation system or recommendation platform) is a subclass of information filtering systems that seeks to predict the rating or preference a user would give to an item.


Recommender systems are everywhere: in movie/series streaming platforms (e.g., Netflix), e-commerce websites (e.g., Amazon), social network platforms (e.g., Facebook, LinkedIn), or dating apps. These systems typically leverage historical data to automatically recommend items or products that a user is likely to be interested in.



So, let's consider how those recommender systems are constructed. A useful starting point is the *non-personalized* baseline that many platforms still display: top-5 lists. A few years ago, the recommendations you could find were about top-5 destinations for the summer, top-5 Black Friday deals, and so on. Those lists are based on expert knowledge or aggregate statistics, and they lack personalization. This is exactly where recommender systems come in.

In this section, we explore fundamental recommendation methods: content-based methods, collaborative filtering (item-based or user-based), and latent factor models. If we classify the different methods, we notice that they are based on mainly two types of information: (i) characteristics or information about the items, and/or (ii) user-item interactions. This approach leads to

* <font color=blue>**Content-based methods**</font>: focusing on attributes of a specific item.

* <font color=blue>**Collaborative Filtering**</font> (item-based / user-based) methods: based on the analysis of user-item interaction data.

* <font color=blue>**Baseline predictors**</font>: global, user, and item effects as a first model for the rating matrix.

* <font color=blue>**Latent Factor Models**</font>: also based on the analysis of user-item interaction data.

Hybrid methods combine content-based ideas with collaborative filtering, and modern production systems often use deep learning. We mention those only briefly at the end; the rest of this chapter develops the three families above.

Several of these ideas were sharpened in industry, notably around the **Netflix Prize** (2006--2009), a public competition that asked teams to predict movie ratings and scored them by RMSE. Matrix factorization became a standard latent-factor method in large part because of that competition.





## Content-Based Methods


The content-based method is the more intuitive of the two classical approaches. Assume that we are an online bookstore and we want a catalogue in which every item (book) can be represented accurately. We represent each book as a multidimensional feature vector. The features could include the author, the publisher, the genre, and the year---anything that we believe describes the type of book---and the resulting vector is the *item profile*. We then visualize every item as a distinct point within a multidimensional feature space (the orange dots in the figure).

```{r ,echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align="center", out.width="30%", fig.cap="User and Item feature space"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/week11/useritem.png")
```

We keep a bank of item profiles, and we also construct a *user profile* in the same feature space (the green dots in the figure). Building the user profile is harder. Typically this is done either *directly*, by asking users for feedback, or *indirectly*, by monitoring activity on the website (clicks, viewing times, and analysis of items the user has already interacted with). These profiles usually give more weight to recent interactions than to older ones. The recommendation is then based on the items that are **closer** to the user in this multidimensional feature space. In other words, <font color=blue>*closeness equates to preference*</font>, which gives us a way to make tailored recommendations.


**Advantages.** The main advantage of this approach is that it does not require any other user's data to make a recommendation. It is therefore possible to start recommending from day one, without waiting for an expensive collection of user-item interaction data. The method also does not discriminate on the basis of item popularity: a rare book and a bestseller are treated the same way if they sit at the same distance from the user. Recommendations are tied to explicit features, which makes the system relatively transparent. It is easy to say why an item was recommended (matching author, genre, and so on) and how it aligns with the user's interests.

**Limitations.** The same mechanism produces *limited discovery*. Because every recommendation is based on items similar to those the user has already interacted with, the system tends to keep suggesting more of the same and rarely surfaces something unexpected. New users with empty profiles are also hard to place in the feature space until some feedback has been collected.




## Collaborative Filtering


The collaborative filtering method relies on an interaction matrix between users and items, known as <font color=darkblue>**the rating matrix**</font>. This is an $m \times n$ grid, where rows represent users and columns represent items. Within this matrix, some entries are known via *explicit* or *implicit* feedback. Explicit feedback might be direct ratings, such as a user's rating of a movie on Netflix on a scale from one to five. Implicit feedback comes from behavior such as clicking on an item or spending time viewing a particular movie, which provides only indirect clues about preference.



Mathematically, the problem we need to solve is *matrix completion*: we fill in the blanks by predicting preferences for items a user has not yet interacted with. Throughout, we write $r_{aj}=?$ when user $a$ has no observed rating for item $j$.


```{r ,echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align="center", out.width="45%"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/week11/ratingmatrix.png")
```

There are two types of collaborative filtering:

* <font color=blue>**User-based CF**</font>: "*Similar users will like similar items.*" For example, if User A liked an item and User B has a similar profile to User A, it is likely that User B will also like that item. The challenge is defining what makes users similar.

* <font color=blue>**Item-based CF**</font>: "*Users will like items similar to those they have already liked.*" For example, if User A liked Item X, and Item Y is similar to Item X, then User A is likely to like Item Y as well.



#### User-based Collaborative Filtering {-}

The challenge in user-based collaborative filtering is to quantify resemblance between users (or, later, items) even when most ratings are missing. This means that we need a notion of **similarity**. Some of the most commonly used similarity metrics include:


* <font color=blue>**Jaccard Similarity**</font>: compares users based on the items they have both interacted with, or compares items based on shared users. It is ideal for binary data. For explicit ratings one first binarizes (for example, "rated" versus "not rated", or "liked" versus "not liked"):
\[\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}, \quad \text{where } A, B \text{ are two sets.}\]


* <font color=blue>**Cosine Similarity**</font>: measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors. Missing values are ignored, or equivalently treated as zeros:
\[\frac{u^{\top} v}{\|u\| \cdot \|v\|}, \quad \text{where } u,v \text{ are two vectors.}\]

* <font color=blue>**Centered Cosine Similarity (Pearson Correlation)**</font>:
A variation of cosine similarity that first subtracts a user's (or item's) mean rating:
\[\frac{(u-\bar{u})^{\top} (v-\bar{v})}{\|u-\bar{u}\| \cdot \|v-\bar{v}\|}, \quad \text{where } u,v \text{ are two vectors.}\]

<br><br>

Cosine and Pearson coefficients fall in the range $[-1, 1]$, whereas a similarity used as a weight is often expected to lie in $[0, 1]$. Negative similarities are awkward in a weighted average, so in practice one either keeps only positive similarities or maps the coefficient to $[0,1]$ via $(1+\cos)/2$. In what follows we treat the similarity $s_{au}$ as a weight and assume that convention has already been chosen.

The measures are computed from the *shared*, non-missing elements between two entities. For users $u$ and $v$, the calculation uses only items that both users have rated. Consequently the effective length of the vector for $u$ can change depending on whether we compare $u$ with $v_1$ or $u$ with $v_2$. A common pathology is that two users who have rated only one item in common receive similarity $1$.

Two conventions for centering are in use, and they are not the same:

* **Center on all of a user's ratings, then take cosine on co-rated items.** If user $u$ has rated 20 movies and 5 of those are also rated by user $v$, the mean $\bar{u}$ is computed from all 20 ratings, while the cosine uses only the 5 shared ratings. This is the usual implementation of Pearson correlation in recommender systems.
* **Restrict everything, including the means, to co-rated items.** In the same example, both the centering and the cosine use only the 5 shared ratings.

The displayed formula above corresponds to the second convention if $\bar{u}$ and $\bar{v}$ are computed on the co-rated support only. Finally, the denominator can become zero when all non-missing entries of a (centered) vector are constant, so those pairs must be skipped or regularized.




```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align="center", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="65%"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/week11/ucbf.png")
```




In the illustration above we used simple averages. We can extend this to **weighted averages**, using weights based on proximity to the user of interest. Let $N(a)$ be the set of $k$ nearest neighbors of user $a$. The predicted rating of user $a$ for item $i$ is

\[
\hat{r}_{ai}
=
\frac{
\sum_{u \in N(a):\, r_{ui} \neq ?} s_{au}\, r_{ui}
}{
\sum_{u \in N(a):\, r_{ui} \neq ?} s_{au}
}.
\]

The prediction is undefined if no neighbor of $a$ has rated item $i$. In practice, to reduce that problem, we select the nearest neighbors *among users who have rated the item in question*. The neighborhood of $a$ may therefore change with $i$. A mean-centered variant replaces $r_{ui}$ by $r_{ui}-\bar{r}_u$ and then adds $\bar{r}_a$ back after the weighted average.



<br>


#### Item-Based Collaborative Filtering {-}


In item-based collaborative filtering, we consider similarities between items instead of users. Below, a similarity matrix for items is constructed.

```{r ,echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align="center", out.width="65%"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/week11/icbf.png")
```

The top three entries in each row are highlighted in bold, since we consider only 3-nearest neighbors. For a test user, represented in orange, who has provided ratings for items 1, 5, and 8, these respective columns are highlighted in blue. These are the items the test user has rated, and their ratings will serve as the foundation for our predictions.








For the test user in question, the aim is to predict the ratings for the unreviewed items using the known ratings for items 1, 5, and 8.

Let $S(i)$ be the set of $k$ nearest items to item $i$ (in the figure, $k=3$). The **predicted rating** $\hat{r}_{ai}$ for item $i$ from user $a$ is a weighted average of $a$'s ratings on those neighbors that $a$ has actually rated, with weights given by item-item similarities $s_{ij}$:

\[
\hat{r}_{ai}
=
\frac{
\sum_{j \in S(i):\, r_{aj} \neq ?} s_{ij}\, r_{aj}
}{
\sum_{j \in S(i):\, r_{aj} \neq ?} s_{ij}
}.
\]

The prediction is missing if the set $\{j \in S(i): r_{aj} \neq ?\}$ is empty, i.e., when none of the similar items have been rated by the user. As in the user-based case, we can choose the neighbors of $i$ dynamically among items that user $a$ has rated, so that the neighborhood used for $\hat{r}_{ai}$ can depend on $a$.


<br>

#### Pros and Cons of Collaborative Filtering {-}


Collaborative filtering does not rely on pre-defined item features: user interactions *become* the features, so the system can recommend items outside the user's usual content profile.
It cannot start from day one, because it needs a build-up of user-item interaction data. New items with no interaction history cannot be recommended; this is the **cold start** problem (the same issue appears for brand-new users). There is also a risk of popularity bias, in which items that many people have already rated are recommended to everyone and personalization is weakened.

<br>

#### Item-Based vs User-Based Collaborative Filtering {-}


The choice between user-based and item-based collaborative filtering often depends on the specific context and platform.

For instance, e-commerce sites and streaming services such as Amazon and Netflix have often found item-based CF more effective. Item similarities tend to be more stable over time than user similarities, and "users who liked this also liked that" is a more reliable relation than the less predictable notion of similar people.

Neither algorithm is cheap if one identifies nearest neighbors by a brute-force scan of a large catalog. Approximation algorithms, clustering, and efficient data structures are used to keep the cost manageable.



Item-based CF also has a *computational* advantage in production. Both methods must find nearest neighbors, but item-based CF can push most of the work into an offline training phase: one builds and sorts an item-to-item similarity matrix once, then serves predictions from it. User-based CF has no comparable static training phase; similarities between users are computed at prediction time, which is expensive in real time.

The tradeoff is memory. The precomputed item-item matrix must be stored and accessed efficiently when recommendations are generated. If the catalog is huge one typically keeps only the top-$k$ similarities per item.


<br>



## Baseline Predictors


Before we go to latent factors, it is useful to look at a much simpler model. Some users rate everything highly, some items are universally liked, and there is an overall average level of ratings. So a natural first prediction for a missing entry is not a neighbor or a latent factor, but a *baseline*.

Start with the global average of all observed ratings, \(\mu\). Then allow each user their own offset \(a_i\) and each item its own offset \(b_j\):

\[
\hat{R}_{ij} = \mu + a_i + b_j.
\]

This is just a regression on dummy variables for users and items, fit only on the observed entries. We can think of a ladder of baselines:

- predict everything by the global mean \(\mu\),
- then by a user mean \(\mu + a_i\),
- then by an item mean \(\mu + b_j\),
- then by \(\mu + a_i + b_j\).

Already this removes a lot of the obvious structure in the rating matrix. The residual

\[
\tilde{R}_{ij} = R_{ij} - \mu - a_i - b_j
\]

is what neighborhood methods or latent factors should be asked to explain. In that sense, collaborative filtering and matrix factorization are models for the leftover, not for the raw stars.

We usually regularize \(a_i\) and \(b_j\) as well, especially for users or items with very few ratings --- the same shrinkage idea as in penalized regression. A user who has rated only one movie should not get a huge \(a_i\).


<br>



## Latent Factor Model


The latent factor model is another way to work with the rating matrix. The idea is inspired by a truncated singular value decomposition (SVD): we approximate the $m \times n$ rating matrix by a product of two thinner factor matrices that embed users and items in a shared $d$-dimensional space.

 
```{r ,echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align="center", out.width="65%"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/week11/latent.png")
```

The decomposition is
\[
R_{m \times n} \approx U_{m \times d}\, V^{\top}_{d \times n},
\]
where $V$ is $n \times d$. The $d$ columns of $U$ are user factors and the $d$ columns of $V$ (equivalently, the $d$ rows of $V^{\top}$) are item factors. A user's predicted preference for an item is the inner product of the corresponding factor vectors. In a full SVD one would also have a diagonal matrix of singular values; here those scales are absorbed into $U$ and $V$.


Classical SVD cannot be applied directly, because $R$ has missing entries. Instead we minimize a quadratic loss *only over observed ratings*. If every entry were observed, that minimizer would recover (a truncation of) the ordinary SVD. To avoid overfitting we add penalty terms on the factors. The resulting objective is

\[
\sum_{R_{ij} \neq ?} \bigl(R_{ij} - u_i^{\top} v_j\bigr)^2 + \lambda_1 \mathrm{Pen}(U) + \lambda_2 \mathrm{Pen}(V),
\]

where $u_i$, the $i$-th row of $U$, is the latent vector for user $i$, and $v_j$, the $j$-th row of $V$, is the latent vector for item $j$. Typical penalties are squared Frobenius norms, $\mathrm{Pen}(U)=\|U\|_F^2$ and $\mathrm{Pen}(V)=\|V\|_F^2$.

This loss is convex in $U$ for fixed $V$ and convex in $V$ for fixed $U$, but it is **not jointly convex** in $(U,V)$. In practice one therefore uses alternating least squares (ALS), cycling between the two blocks, or stochastic gradient descent over observed ratings. After the factors have been fit, a missing entry is predicted by the inner product $u_i^{\top} v_j$.



Taking this model further, we put the baseline from the previous section back in. The latent product is then asked only to explain what is left after $\mu + a_i + b_j$:

\[
R_{ij} = \underbrace{\mu}_{\text{Overall Average} } + \underbrace{a_i}_{\text{User Effect}} + \underbrace{b_j}_{\text{Item Effect}} + u_i^{\top} v_j.
\]

Substituting that into the loss, and regularizing $a$ and $b$ as well, gives

\[
\sum_{R_{ij} \neq ?}
\bigl(R_{ij} - \mu - a_i - b_j - u_i^{\top} v_j\bigr)^2
+ \lambda\bigl(\|U\|_F^2 + \|V\|_F^2 + \|a\|_2^2 + \|b\|_2^2\bigr).
\]

The same ALS or SGD procedures apply. In practice the baseline alone already does a lot; the factors are there to capture the leftover user--item interactions.


<br>

## Evaluating Recommender Systems


Evaluation is often treated as a prediction task, but the way we *split* the data matters as much as the metric.

The unit of splitting is a *rating*, not a row of a table. If we randomly shuffle users the way we did in classification, we can leak a user's later ratings into the training set and then "predict" their earlier ones. A standard protocol is:

- hold out some observed entries,  at random, or better, the most recent ratings of each user,
- fit the model on the remaining observed entries only,
- score only the held-out cells.

RMSE (and MAE) make sense when the system is really asked to predict a number of stars. RMSE was the official score of the Netflix Prize, and it is still the default number people report. It has drawbacks. In many cases we care more about higher ratings (such as 4 or 5) that signal strong interest, and about what appears at the *top of a list*. Ranking metrics such as Precision@$K$, Recall@$K$, or NDCG@$K$ are usually closer to how recommendations are actually shown.

One more warning: when we compute Precision@$K$ we have to decide what counts as a "relevant" item among the ones the user never saw. Held-out high ratings are the usual proxy. That proxy is imperfect, which is one reason live experiments still matter once a system is in production.


<br>

## Challenges & Strategies


1. <font color=darkblue> **Computational Efficiency:**</font><br>
To find similar items or users efficiently, a pre-clustering step is often used. By grouping users into clusters beforehand, the search for the most similar user can be restricted to the same cluster, which reduces computational overhead.

2. <font color=darkblue> **Combining Multiple Systems:**</font><br>
In practice, recommender systems often combine several approaches. For instance, Amazon may showcase the week's top deals, popular products within specific categories, and items you have previously shown interest in. This hybrid strategy accommodates different user preferences and different data constraints (including cold start).

3. <font color=darkblue> **Contextual Information:**</font><br>
Modern recommendation systems also take contextual factors into account---a user's location, time of access, and device (e.g., phone, computer, or tablet). The browsing context often changes what a good recommendation is.

4. <font color=darkblue> **Evaluating Recommender Systems:**</font><br>
See the previous section. The short version: split by held-out *ratings* (ideally the most recent ones), report RMSE if you are predicting stars, and report a ranking metric such as Precision@$K$ if you are producing a list.

5. <font color=darkblue> **Balance between accuracy and diversity:**</font> <br>
Accuracy matters, but so does diversity. If every recommendation is a near-duplicate of something the user already likes, the list is precise and still unhelpful. Serendipity---helping users discover unexpected items they end up enjoying---is part of what makes a system feel useful.

6. <font color=darkblue> **Incorporating User Feedback:**</font><br>
It is important to distinguish a user's lack of interest in an item from mere unawareness of it. Tracking clicks (and skips) on recommended items provides feedback that ratings alone do not.

7. <font color=darkblue> **Challenges in Recommendation Systems:**</font><br>
Scalability and data sparsity remain the main engineering constraints. The cold-start problem---how to recommend for a new user, or how to promote a newly added item---has no single universal solution; it is usually handled by mixing content-based signals, popularity baselines, and the collaborative or latent-factor models of this chapter.
